source.verification_method: All 60 supplied pages inspected. Image-only questionnaire and delegate profiles on PDF pages 38–49 read visually; equations on pages 21 and 26 also inspected visually. Bibliographic identity read from the supplied covers.

citation.title: Delegating Moral Dilemmas in Autonomous Vehicles Evidence from an online experiment in China

reading.source_scope_note: Human online hypothetical vehicle dilemmas with delegation to depicted human doctor, elder or authority profiles. No human-versus-AI delegate comparison, implemented AV decision system, actual injury, delegation fee or identified avoidance mechanism.
access_limits: All extracted text read; image-only pages 38–49 read from page renders, including all 18 scenarios, 13 background questions and three delegate profiles. Missing extracted equations were read visually on pages 21 and 26.

Original Mandarin questionnaire, OSF raw data and scripts, recruitment denominators and final journal version were not independently examined. Referenced control-premium and betrayal-aversion primary studies are secondary citations here, not separately read papers.

study.sample: 418 valid complete online responses recruited through Weibo/WeChat, 2–11 July 2020: doctor 94, elder 99, authority 127, baseline 98. Nominal 320 people can delegate, generating 5,760 repeated scenario choices; all groups generate 7,524 choices. No data on incomplete or declining respondents.
study.design: Random assignment to one of four between-person conditions; 18 fixed-order scenarios per person. Baseline offers straight/left; other groups add a human delegate. Profiles additionally promise more casualty information, experience or responsibility-taking. Text and cartoons jointly vary.
study.measures: Hypothetical choice; self-reported demographic/driving variables; hypothetical 100-unit dictator allocation; general and domain risk willingness; interpersonal trust, all background questions after the dilemmas.
study.results: 53.82% of delegation-available choices are delegated: doctor 55.79%, elder 50.51%, authority 54.94%. This is a repeated-choice aggregate, not the percentage of people who usually delegate. Profile differences are not detected. Main-text six baseline-versus-nondelegator contrasts conflict with seven nominally significant scenarios in Appendix Table VII.
study.analysis: Binary panel logit for delegation versus no delegation; nested logit additionally models straight versus left. Many subgroup coefficients and nominal tests; tables generally omit standard errors/intervals. Model rankings rely on AIC/BIC for differently defined outcomes.

summary: Add decision delegation, control premium and betrayal aversion, with direct choice evidence distinguished from secondary definitions. Record that human delegate profiles are not AI delegates; non-detected contrasts do not establish equivalence, intrinsic avoidance motives or unchanged moral preferences. Correct a misuse of the existing moral-crumple-zone label in a boundary note.

findings.definition: Transferring decision-making authority to another party who chooses on one's behalf.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Direct hypothetical human delegation choices to human profiles in vehicle dilemmas; application to AI workflows is proposed rather than directly compared
findings.ai_proposal: Distinguish asking an AI for advice from authorizing it to choose or act. Record the delegated decision, limits, retained oversight, intervention options and accountable parties; test whether people delegate because of expected competence, effort, distress or responsibility concerns rather than infer a motive from the choice alone.
findings.novelty_rationale: Authority transfer differs from taking an advisor's recommendation as a reason, responsibility displacement, automation overreliance and illusory control. The existing ontology contains related consequences and motives but no general delegation entry.

evidence.quote: decision-making power to a third party who then acts on our behalf.
most participants (53.82%) choose to delegate their decision-making power.
Another key limitation of our research is the inability to explore the mechanisms behind the

findings.evidence_scope: Explicit definition and repeated human choices. The aggregate 53.82% applies to choices across 320 delegation-eligible participants and 18 scenarios. Options nominate a doctor, elder or authority; no actual AI delegate decides or delivers outcomes. Avoidance mechanisms are acknowledged as unexamined.
findings.boundary: Delegation can be justified and consensual. It need not imply blind trust, abdication, blame evasion, loss of all control or transfer of legal accountability. Advice, authority transfer and execution are separate stages. A model may delegate a subtask without having a human motive or felt moral burden.

findings.definition: A willingness to incur a cost to retain personal decision-making authority or control.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit secondary concept in the fully read background; no willingness-to-pay or control-premium estimate in this study
findings.ai_proposal: Measure what users are willing to trade to retain final decision authority in otherwise comparable AI-assisted tasks. Separate the intrinsic value of choosing from expected differences in quality, privacy, accountability or safety, and preserve legitimate preferences for oversight.
findings.novelty_rationale: Valuing actual decision rights is distinct from falsely believing one controls chance, refusing correction or preferring one's own reasoning regardless of quality. It is not synonymous with every form of algorithm aversion.

evidence.quote: assert that people willingly and consciously pay a control premium to
retain decision-making power and maintain control.

findings.evidence_scope: The introduction defines a paid preference for control through Owens et al. (2014) and decision-rights literature. Delegation is free here, so the experiment neither estimates this premium nor establishes its absence when people delegate.
findings.boundary: Choosing oversight is not inherently irrational. A measured premium can combine intrinsic autonomy with expectations about performance or consequences unless the design separates them. The original cited experiment has not been read; one secondary article is not several direct replications or proof an AI subjectively values control.

findings.definition: Additional reluctance to accept vulnerability when a bad outcome could result from another party's betrayal rather than an otherwise comparable impersonal risk.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit secondary human preference discussed in background; not manipulated or separately measured in this vehicle experiment
findings.ai_proposal: In human–AI reliance studies, distinguish aversion to an unfavorable random outcome from aversion to a perceived violation of an entrusted role. Match outcome probabilities and stakes where feasible; investigate attribution without assuming a model has intentions or that users' legitimate accountability concerns are errors.
findings.novelty_rationale: The source of uncertainty and perceived violation of trust matter beyond generic loss, ambiguity or anticipated regret. It is not an alias for all reluctance to use an algorithm.

evidence.quote: risk. Individuals tend to be more risk-averse when uncertainty arises from the actions of other
more strongly to betrayal compared to similar negative outcomes without betrayal

findings.evidence_scope: The literature discussion distinguishes interpersonal betrayal from impersonal risk and cites Bohnet/Zeckhauser, Bohnet et al., Aimone/Houser and Koehler/Gershoff. This experiment has no matched human/random-source manipulation or measured betrayal response; its trust null does not test betrayal aversion.
findings.boundary: Interpersonal uncertainty, intentional wrongdoing, legitimate distrust and objectively worse reliability are different. An AI error is not automatically betrayal, intentional malice or proof of a human-like mind. The cited primary studies and their alternative operational definitions remain unread.

findings.term: Moral crumple zone label is misapplied to reduced outrage at AI
findings.definition: Disproportionate responsibility imposed on a low-control human operator is distinct from simply expressing less outrage at a machine.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserve the existing narrower definition rather than importing the article's broader and misleading label as a new synonym or independent replication.

evidence.quote: be driven by biases, a concept known as the "moral crumple zone"

findings.evidence_scope: The background links reduced outrage over AI discrimination to Elish's label without establishing a human operator disproportionately absorbs blame despite limited control. The current delegation questionnaire does not measure such responsibility allocation.
findings.boundary: Reduced AI blame alone is insufficient to identify a moral crumple zone. Inspect actual authority, information, intervention opportunity and allocation of responsibility to humans. This terminology correction is a boundary note and does not count as corroborating empirical evidence.

findings.term: Going straight does not uniquely identify omission bias
findings.definition: A preference for the straight option can reflect both fixed spatial presentation and the bundled attributes of the people harmed, rather than an isolated preference for inaction.
findings.novelty_rationale: Do not create a new straight-ahead bias from a confounded choice format or treat it as a clean replication of an action–inaction mechanism.

findings.evidence_scope: The 18 scenarios retain fixed order and fixed side-to-victim mappings. The visual appendix confirms straight appears first/left and turn second/right, with varying victim profiles. No independent action/inaction or side counterbalancing is reported.
findings.boundary: Selecting straight is an explicit decision and can be morally reasoned. Choice frequency alone cannot separate default, omission, position, population or victim-attribute effects. The study is not counted as direct evidence uniquely establishing omission bias.

methodological_limits: The human-profile delegation experiment is framed around AVs but does not compare human and AI delegates, produce an autonomous decision, or measure actual crash outcomes. Its preference rate cannot be generalized directly to willingness to delegate to AI.

The reported 53.82% is an aggregate of repeated choices. It does not establish that 53.82% of people usually delegate, that most people delegate on every scenario, or that the option is intrinsically preferred independent of expected quality/cost.

H1 shifts between majority and plurality. In 2lawbreak2doct, 5cat1eld and 3lawbreak1lawabid, straight exceeds delegation; the claim delegation is the most frequent option in all scenarios is contradicted by Table 2.

The abstract/highlights imply unchanged moral standards. Comparison of baseline respondents with only those who choose not to delegate conditions on a post-treatment choice; it is not a full-sample intention-to-treat estimate of a stable latent moral preference. Non-detection is also not equivalence.

The main text names six significant straight/left changes. Appendix Table VII additionally lists 5cat1eld at chi-square p=.005/Fisher p=.006, making seven nominally significant scenarios. The list and its 12-of-18 unchanged count need reconciliation. No multiplicity correction across the scenario family is stated.

Doctor, elder and authority conditions bundle role, cartoon, promised information, experience and responsibility capacity. The claim that only iconic names are given is incomplete: actual profiles make explicit additional promises. A cartoon does not guarantee absence of appearance bias.

Undetected delegate-profile contrasts are not equivalence tests and do not establish expertise, appearance or status never matters. All profiles may be viewed as credible; no incompetent, random or unqualified delegate is tested.

The authors explicitly acknowledge the inability to investigate delegation mechanisms. Avoided blame, effort, regret and moral burden are plausible interpretations, not identified mediators; no direct burden or anticipated-blame scale is reported.

All scenarios and blocks have fixed order. Victim age, number, occupation, law compliance, severity, position and action are bundled; several scenarios in the uncertainty block have no uncertain outcome. Block non-detection does not isolate uncertainty as a cause.

Victim-attribute shares across post hoc significance groups are descriptive summaries, not separately randomized causal attribute effects. A normative right to prioritize people by sex, profession, age, disability or lawbreaking does not follow from preferences.

The binary model predicts delegate versus no-delegate; nested logit additionally predicts which nondelegated option is chosen. Their AIC/BIC values use different outcome likelihoods and are not directly comparable evidence that the binary model is superior without a common likelihood and sample basis.

Nested logit permits correlation within a nest but is not free of every IIA-related restriction. No reported estimated dissimilarity parameter, within-nest specification test or common-outcome comparison independently establishes its assumptions here.

The panel equation visually shows a logistic response without an explicit individual random effect; exact fitting and dependence handling require code. Repeated choices are not thousands of independent people. Simple pooled block chi-square/Fisher tests also require attention to clustering.

Many coefficient tables omit SEs and intervals. Sparse demographic/preference categories and very large odds ratios, including altruism OR 114.535, need cell counts and stability checks before interpretation. Odds ratios are not probability ratios.

Reference-category odds ratios in Appendix VIII-2 are printed as 0.000, whereas a baseline contrast normally has exp(0)=1. Several significance stars differ between corresponding coefficient and OR tables, e.g. risk-tolerance levels 2 and 4; exponentiation alone cannot change the same underlying coefficient test.

Gender dictionary codes female=1 and male=0, but the summary reports mean=.73 and the prose says 73% male. These cannot all describe that coding. Do not silently reverse labels or generalize sex effects before checking data.

The dictator item offers 11 allocations including 100/0 and 0/100. The variable is described as 0–10, but summary min/max are 1–10 and regression categories are 1–10. Exact recoding and missing endpoints require clarification before interpreting nonlinearity.

Nested logit includes one numeric profession coefficient although occupations are nominal categories. Coding-dependent rank assumptions can explain disagreement with categorical doctor comparisons; do not interpret the numeric slope as a general doctor effect.

The trust coefficient for strangers is nominally significant in the nested model although the narrative emphasizes no trust effect from the binary model. Model-dependent findings should not be flattened into a universal absence of association.

Demographics, trust, altruism and risk scores are observational and measured after choices; associations are not causal effects of sex, education, profession or personality. They do not justify profiling who should surrender decision authority.

Social-media recruitment, completion-only submission, group imbalances and no decline/incomplete denominator limit representativeness. Random assignment within this sample is not random sampling of China, Asia or all drivers. Broad cultural stereotypes in the background are not measured results.

Participation is compensated 10 RMB, but choices and the dictator allocation have no described consequence-contingent monetary implementation. Calling the study wholly without monetary incentives would miss the participation fee; it remains a stated-preference design.
No delegation fees or willingness-to-pay conditions are included. Popularity of free delegation cannot refute an intrinsic value of control or estimate a control premium.
Cronbach alpha=.805 for unspecified items does not by itself validate a heterogeneous questionnaire or guarantee reliability of every scale and observed choice.

Several main-text years disagree with the same reference list, including Kraetschmer 2014 versus 2004, Xia 2014 versus 2004, and Wallberg 2009 versus 2000. These are internal discrepancies; primary metadata was not independently checked in this review.

The supplied English baseline instruction says three choices despite displaying two. Actual Mandarin delivery is not independently checked. This appendix ambiguity is not evidence of a third baseline choice or of participant misunderstanding.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Moral advice acceptance and transferring choice authority are different interventions. A recipient can use advice while retaining the decision; a delegator need not adopt the delegate's reasoning as a personal moral belief.

Fixed aggressive/conservative recommendations retain human choice authority, unlike the current delegation option. Felt responsibility, actual transfer and willingness to use support should be measured separately.

The existing moral-crumple-zone definition concerns a low-control human absorbing disproportionate blame. The present background's reduced-outrage-at-AI use is insufficient and is retained as a terminology warning rather than corroboration.

As with option-set sensitivity in equal-chance preference, a third option changes the choice environment. Baseline-versus-selected nondelegator ratios do not automatically reveal an unchanged intrinsic moral ordering.

deferred.reason: Discussed as an explanation overlapping existing experiential avoidance, regret aversion and responsibility displacement. The current design explicitly cannot identify motives; a new pathological subtype is not justified.

Cost, competence beliefs, anticipated burden and institutional context are not separated. Retain the general decision-delegation entry rather than promote an interpretation into an independently measured mechanism.
Fixed side/order and victim characteristics are confounded; related omission and position concepts already exist.

limitations: Three additions include one directly elicited choice behavior and two explicitly secondary concepts. They are not three proven AI defects; no ethical violation or harm edges are automatically added.
